context: From [0, 0] in a grid of nonnegative numbers, we can move only right or down. Let dp[i, j] be the minimum path sum to row i, column j, with indices starting at 0. This search also starts at dp[2, 1] and shows how a cache, mem, prunes overlapping subproblems. The grid weights are unspecified. Recursion looks backward to predecessors in the previous row and column, opposite to the down and right directions of travel.

For a valid interior state, take the smaller predecessor result and add the current cell cost: dp[i, j] = min(dp[i-1, j], dp[i, j-1]) + grid[i, j]. The starting cell returns grid[0, 0], and an out-of-bounds negative index returns positive infinity.
description: The left branch of the recursion tree checks the previous row (“up”), and the right branch checks the previous column (“left”). The route labels describe directions in the grid, independently of the branches' positions in the drawing.
From root dp[2,1], the path through dp[1,1] to dp[1,0] is “up→left.” The path through dp[2,0] to dp[1,0] is “left→up.” Both request the same subproblem.

Solve the dp[1,1] branch first. On the first visit to dp[1,0], wait for both predecessor calls to return, calculate the minimum path sum to the current cell, and write it to mem[1][0]. Only then return to dp[1,1]. Next, solve the dp[2,0] branch. Its request for dp[1,0] hits the cache (“Prune: result already cached”) and returns the stored value without calling dp[0,0] or dp[1,-1]. The other child of dp[2,0], dp[2,-1] on the “left→left” route, is out of bounds and returns positive infinity. The cached value is a valid path sum and participates in the minimum comparison.

The search visits six valid states in rows 0–2 and columns 0–1: [0,0], [0,1], [1,0], [1,1], [2,0], and [2,1]. Both dp[0,1] and the first call to dp[1,0] call the starting cell dp[0,0] once, along “up→up→left” and “up→left→up.” The starting cell returns grid[0,0] without reading or writing mem, so both starting-cell leaves remain. The table below lists all calls in order: enter the node, check above, then check left. This diagram has no separate grid or dp table.

frames.explanation: Omitting the two children of the second dp[1,0] reduces the call count from 13 in brute-force search to 11. The table retains two calls to the starting cell dp[0,0] and three out-of-bounds calls, dp[-1,1], dp[1,-1], and dp[2,-1].
frames.title: Reusing dp[1, 0] on a cache hit and distinguishing it from out-of-bounds pruning

summary: The second request for dp[1,0] reads the valid cached path sum directly, without expanding its children. An out-of-bounds call instead returns positive infinity.
